P1.evidence: The best opening in the batch. Setter notes read back explicitly and used to build rapport: 'I've gone through the call that you had with Kim a few days ago. So I have a roughly understanding what's your situation. However, I'm kind of old school, and I'm 43, like you. So I like to hear it from the person directly.' The frame ran three of four parts — what's going on, what you're trying to achieve, and the conditional promise 'if there's an alignment there, I will tell you exactly how we can actually help you get there' — with nothing on what is in the way. Frame agreement was sought and given: 'Sounds good.' The open question landed and produced a five-minute unprompted answer covering structure, energy, belly fat and the abandoned application form.

P2.evidence: Age carried over from setter notes; height and weight never asked. Work covered exceptionally — desk time, commute, office days, and then the rep had him open the Apple Health app live and read his own step counts aloud: '1,942. The other day, did 3,218, 2,532.' That is a better baseline artefact than anything else in the batch. Health conditions were never asked, which is the critical failure of this phase: the sudden hearing loss surfaced forty minutes later under the why question, entirely unprompted, and by the rule that counts as a miss. Injuries asked only as sitting-related stiffness with no duration. Training week captured in detail including bell weights and rep counts. Energy was probed properly and twice: 'you mentioned you have those energy level drops during the day. Or is it that you wake up already kind of groggy?' and 'when did you notice that? Is it that something recent or that's something that's been going on for a longer period?' Sleep only touched via the grogginess question. Diet covered fully including the guilty-pleasure question.

P3.evidence: The bridge question was clean, patient and open, and it is what produced the most important disclosure on the call: 'in your own words, if you'd have to think about it for a second, like, what would be your biggest why for this? What's the main driver?' The answer was the February hearing loss and 'I don't think I've ever unlocked my real potential. And I really want to do that this time.' Mobility, strength and energy were all worked, with the rep narrowing to core and lower body: 'you would say that lower body needs more attention than upper body right now?' The can't-do-physically question was never asked and the moving-better question was never asked. Who-else-does-it-impact was led rather than asked — the rep raised the children himself. The legacy drive-through and the reflect-back both landed: 'there's this bigger why and not just superficial, you know, I want to be lean and have a six-pack. That's nice, but that's a byproduct.' — 'Exactly.'

P4.evidence: Weakest phase and the most consequential gap. The prospect handed over his own root cause unprompted and precisely — 'I work well as a team, when I'm an individual, right? That's where I don't think my A game comes out well. And someone who can push me is what I'm looking for' — and the rep never asked a single follow-up about why that is, what has failed before, or what happened when he tried. Past attempts came out only in passing (Instagram sources, previous online programmes) and were never systematically asked for; the fact that he abandoned the application form halfway went unexamined despite being a live demonstration of the exact pattern. P4f was substituted with a reframe rather than a question: 'When you think about an athlete, he has a coach for his fitness, for his mindset, for everything... So why would you not invest in yourself?' That argues the case instead of making the prospect articulate it.

P5.evidence: No consequence frame ran. Not one of the four moves appears. In its place the rep used two pieces of generic fear content — a secondhand claim that '50% of prevention from cancer is actually movement' attributed to a cancer lab researcher, and 'sitting is like smoking of 21st century right now' — neither of which asks the prospect to describe his own two-year trajectory or to reject it. A prospect who had just disclosed an unexplained sensory loss at 43 was maximally primed for this phase and it was skipped entirely, which is why the price landed against a budget rather than against a cost.

P6.evidence: Both questions ran and ran in the right order, before the price. Belief: 'I understand that if you had this right training, the simple nutrition, and the guidance and accountability from Trevor, do you feel you would get, finally, to your goals?' — 'I think so, absolutely.' All-in: 'if we can figure out all the logistical details, are you fully committed to showing up, actually, and doing the work?' But the answer was not a clear yes — 'That is the most important question... But I think I mentioned this to Kim as well, you know, the cost factor also plays' — and the script requires returning to Phase 5 at exactly that point. Instead the rep ran a plane-oxygen-mask analogy and went straight to the number. Phase 5 had never run, so there was nothing to return to.

P11.evidence: A close was attempted: two financing configurations were priced live ($650/month and $433/month over twelve months) and a downsell product was offered with a price and cancellation terms. But payment was never actually asked for, no link was confirmed sent, and nothing was collected. Steps two to four were unreachable with no sale — no Trevor onboarding call, no agreement, no Skool or questionnaire instructions for the coaching programme.

objection_plays.detail: Clear trigger — 'I would definitely need to think on this. I can't commit to it in this call, for sure' and later 'maybe I'll sit on it'. No OA move ran. The rep had already banked the answer to 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to your goal?' minutes earlier ('I think so, absolutely') and never used it. 'Thinking isn't the problem, deciding is' and 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here' were both available and both unspoken — the second especially, since the prospect had literally abandoned the application form halfway to think about it after his holiday.

A textbook OB trigger in substance: 'This is something that's, it's a family decision, right? Anything that we put into as an investment has to be talked to on this.' Not one of the six scripted moves ran. No money-aside belief check, no 'when you talk to her, what obstacles might come up?', no 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger?', no 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission to bet on yourself?', and no deposit-with-full-refund fallback — which is the one move that would have fitted a prospect who wanted to buy but needed household sign-off. The rep did not appear to register it as an objection type at all.

The break-it-up move ran and financing was quoted in two configurations. Everything else was skipped. No isolation after the objection landed, no 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no request for an open honest financial conversation, and none of the six financial-picture questions — cash on hand, monthly surplus, number of credit cards, available credit per card, used versus available, investments. The prospect volunteered exactly one number, a $250/month expectation, and the rep never tested whether that was a budget, a habit or a hard ceiling. Having skipped the picture, the rep had nothing left when financing failed and improvised toward asset liquidation.

Weak but present: 'this is on a higher number for me, Andrew, at this point in my life.' No OD move ran and the rep actively conceded the timing rather than challenging it — 'after some time, when you have a better financing situation, we can get back to the conversation.' The script's own line, that things never slow down and the longer you wait the harder it gets, is the direct counter to 'at this point in my life' and was not used.
No fear or doubt about the method or his own capability. He was confident he would follow through and the rep agreed.

Two unscripted improvisations, both worth surfacing as script gaps rather than rep failures. First, there is no scripted downsell, so the rep invented one live — Primal University on Skool at roughly $199/month — with no stated positioning, no bridge back to the one-to-one offer and no defined path between the two, and the prospect rejected it in one sentence because it lacks the accountability he came for. Second, and more seriously, there is no scripted path for a sole-earner with genuine family financial obligations, so the rep reached for asset liquidation: 'Maybe there is something, for example, in your house that you don't use anymore, and you can sell it. We had guys doing garage sales in order to get at least some amount to split it into financing.' The script needs a defined stop point for prospects who have told you they cannot afford it.

notes: The best front half in the batch — setter notes read back, frame agreement obtained, energy probed twice with timing, the Apple Health step count pulled live, and a why question patient enough to surface a February health event — collapsing into the worst back half. Phase 5 was skipped entirely, then a conditional yes was accepted, then three separate objections (think about it, family decision, affordability) landed in ninety seconds and not one scripted move ran against any of them. Coach two things: never ask health conditions late or by implication, because on this call an unexplained sensory loss arrived forty minutes after it should have and was never followed up; and when a prospect says he cannot afford it, that is the end of the financial conversation, not the cue for a garage-sale suggestion.
